style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;align=left;verticalAlign=top;fontSize=16;fontColor=#222222;fontStyle=1;spacing=4;" value="How to read it — follow the numbers" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="30" width="900" x="40" y="1395" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="8GnkyYu86gmeWZfBCCJe-95" parent="1" style="rounded=1;arcSize=6;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fontSize=12;fillColor=#ffffff;strokeColor=#999999;strokeWidth=1.5;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;spacingLeft=8;spacingRight=8;spacingTop=2;spacingBottom=2;" value="<b>Flow (①–⑩, F1–F8)</b><br>① Users reach the system through a Global Traffic Manager.<br>② Region A (primary) serves all traffic; Region B (DR) is pre-deployed and scaled down (warm).<br>③ Database replicates continuously — one writer only. ④ Kafka topics + offsets are mirrored. ⑤ Object storage is synced.<br>⑥ We MEASURE replication lag against RPO — lag IS your real RPO.<br>⑦ Monitoring alerts. ⑧ Incident management finds out: one service, or the whole region? ⑨ An authorized person declares DR.<br>⑩ The runbook runs: declare → freeze → fence → validate → promote → scale → route → verify.<br><br><b>Example:</b> RTO 15 min, RPO 1 min. Replication lag 3 s → within target. If lag grows to 20 min, we are already in breach — and we know it BEFORE the disaster.<br><br><b>Why not just "DNS switches over"?</b> Failover is a distributed operation: stop old writes, check data, promote, start, then route." vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="470" width="610" x="40" y="1435" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="8GnkyYu86gmeWZfBCCJe-96" parent="1" style="rounded=1;arcSize=6;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fontSize=12;fillColor=#ffffff;strokeColor=#999999;strokeWidth=1.5;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;spacingLeft=8;spacingRight=8;spacingTop=2;spacingBottom=2;" value="<b>Architect decisions — say "why A over B"</b><br>1. Start from RTO / RPO, not from AWS or Kafka — the business sets the target.<br>2. HA ≠ DR: HA survives a server, DR survives a whole region.<br>3. Warm standby for most, active-active only where needed — it adds conflicts, latency, complexity.<br>4. The database is the hard part: apps can be rebuilt, the ledger cannot.<br>5. RPO is a measurement (replication lag), watched all the time.<br>6. Detect ≠ declare: one failed health check is not a dead region.<br>7. Controlled failover + single writer + fencing → no split-brain.<br>8. Kafka replay is normal → idempotent consumers + business dedup, not "exactly-once".<br>9. In-flight payments: UNKNOWN → idempotency key + status query, never a blind retry.<br>10. Rehearse the runbook — an untested DR plan is only a hope." vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="470" width="610" x="670" y="1435" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="8GnkyYu86gmeWZfBCCJe-97" parent="1" style="rounded=1;arcSize=6;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fontSize=12;fillColor=#ffffff;strokeColor=#999999;strokeWidth=1.5;align=left;verticalAlign=middle;spacingLeft=8;spacingRight=8;spacingTop=2;spacingBottom=2;" value="<b>Mental model &amp; interview close</b><br><i>Business (RTO/RPO) → Strategy → Replicate → Measure → Detect → Decide → Fence → Promote → Route → Verify</i><br><br><b>Trade-offs we accept</b><br>• Warm standby → we pay for idle capacity<br>• Human-approved failover → slower than automatic (higher RTO) but safe from split-brain<br>• Tighter RPO → closer-to-synchronous replication → higher cost and write latency<br>• Single writer → one region is read-only after failover until re-synced<br><br><b>One-line close:</b> "DR is a business promise (RTO / RPO) made real with replication, a rehearsed runbook, and guardrails against split-brain and double payments."<br><br><b>Honest test:</b> Region A comes back 10 minutes after failover — does it start accepting writes again? It must not: it stays fenced, then re-syncs as the standby." vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="470" width="630" x="1300" y="1435" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </root> </mxGraphModel> </diagram> </mxfile>

div.div: How to read it — follow the numbers

div.div:
Flow (①–⑩, F1–F8)
① Users reach the system through a Global Traffic Manager.
② Region A (primary) serves all traffic; Region B (DR) is pre-deployed and scaled down (warm).
③ Database replicates continuously — one writer only. ④ Kafka topics + offsets are mirrored. ⑤ Object storage is synced.
⑥ We MEASURE replication lag against RPO — lag IS your real RPO.
⑦ Monitoring alerts. ⑧ Incident management finds out: one service, or the whole region? ⑨ An authorized person declares DR.
⑩ The runbook runs: declare → freeze → fence → validate → promote → scale → route → verify.
Example: RTO 15 min, RPO 1 min. Replication lag 3 s → within target. If lag grows to 20 min, we are already in breach — and we know it BEFORE the disaster.
Why not just "DNS switches over"? Failover is a distributed operation: stop old writes, check data, promote, start, then route.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 592px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1662px; margin-left: 660px;

div.div:
Architect decisions — say "why A over B"
1. Start from RTO / RPO, not from AWS or Kafka — the business sets the target.
2. HA ≠ DR: HA survives a server, DR survives a whole region.
3. Warm standby for most, active-active only where needed — it adds conflicts, latency, complexity.
4. The database is the hard part: apps can be rebuilt, the ledger cannot.
5. RPO is a measurement (replication lag), watched all the time.
6. Detect ≠ declare: one failed health check is not a dead region.
7. Controlled failover + single writer + fencing → no split-brain.
8. Kafka replay is normal → idempotent consumers + business dedup, not "exactly-once".
9. In-flight payments: UNKNOWN → idempotency key + status query, never a blind retry.
10. Rehearse the runbook — an untested DR plan is only a hope.

div.div:
Mental model & interview close
Business (RTO/RPO) → Strategy → Replicate → Measure → Detect → Decide → Fence → Promote → Route → Verify
Trade-offs we accept
• Warm standby → we pay for idle capacity
• Human-approved failover → slower than automatic (higher RTO) but safe from split-brain
• Tighter RPO → closer-to-synchronous replication → higher cost and write latency
• Single writer → one region is read-only after failover until re-synced
One-line close: "DR is a business promise (RTO / RPO) made real with replication, a rehearsed runbook, and guardrails against split-brain and double payments."
Honest test: Region A comes back 10 minutes after failover — does it start accepting writes again? It must not: it stays fenced, then re-syncs as the standby.
